power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

#### Code Comments
Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code).
#### Missing Files
All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.
#### Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., './files') instead of absolute file paths (e.g., 'C://Lakens/project_dir/files') as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.
#### Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid `setwd()` in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author's own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No `setwd()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid `install.packages()` in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an `renv.lock`/`DESCRIPTION` for R, a `requirements.txt` for Python). No `install.packages()` calls were found in any of the code files.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 637 columns across 90 data files.
#### Issues Identified

69 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 90 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it. **A script downloads data while it runs.** - README.Rmd - allelefrequencies.py Online files can move, change or disappear. Save the downloaded files, add them to the deposit, and let the script read the saved copies. **A script waits for a person to choose a file, answer a question, or give arguments on the command line.** - cigar_comp.py - compile_gates.py - find_mates.py - summarize_csv.py Nobody can answer when the code is checked automatically. Write the file name into the script, and put the exact command with its arguments in the README. **Metacheck can't automatically establish what caused the error, or how it should be improved.** - trim_cigar.py The error message of each script is in the table above. ### Comparison with the paper Of the 3 statistical tests reported in the paper, 0 were found in the output of the code. text.text: Immune allele frequencies inform disease association mapping, pharmacogenomic guidance, and vaccine design, yet such data are missing for most of the world's groups.

Here we present the Global Atlas of Immune Alleles (GAIA), applying benchmarked genotyping tools across the Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA), Immunoglobulin Heavy Chain Constant (IGHC), and Fc Gamma Receptor (FCGR) loci to whole-genome sequencing data from 20,248 individuals, oversampling sub-Saharan African, Island Southeast Asian, and Pacific groups.

Despite representing fewer than 0.5% of observations in the Allele Frequency Net Database, GAIA expands the database's catalogue by 38%, demonstrating that representation matters more than sample size.
We identify HLA alleles at group-specific frequencies that challenge pharmacogenomic screening recommendations and document disease-risk alleles common in groups lacking clinical guidance.

Finally, we introduce majority allelic diversity (MAD-X), which counts the alleles required for X% of individuals in a group to carry at least one, and show that reaching 90% HLA-B coverage for vaccine design requires up to 2.7 times more alleles in underrepresented groups than in those of Northwest European ancestry.
Immune response receptor genes are among the most polymorphic in the human genome.

These include the classical human leukocyte antigen (HLA) genes, which have tens of thousands of allelic variants 1, 2, 3 , and the immunoglobulin heavy chain constant region locus (IGHC), which contains dozens of highly similar, short gene segments, each with multiple alleles 4, 5, 6 .

text.text: This diversity is functionally essential, enabling recognition of diverse pathogens, determining immune cell isotypes, and influencing outcomes in infection, autoimmunity, and vaccine response 7, 8, 9 .

text.text: Specific HLA alleles affect drug reactions and disease susceptibility.
For example, HLA-B*58:01 predisposes carriers to severe allopurinol reactions 10 and multiple HLA-B*27 subtypes are strongly associated with ankylosing spondylitis 11, 12 .

text.text: Characterizing group-level immune gene variation is therefore critical for global health applications, particularly T cell vaccine design, where candidate peptides must bind HLA molecules expressed in the target group to elicit protective responses 14.

text.text: Despite their importance, these loci have been challenging to study at scale.
Standard short-read variant calling does not adequately capture their diversity due to high sequence homology, tandem repeats, and structural variation 15, 16 .

text.text: Global resources such as the 1000 Genomes Project (1kGP) include diverse groups but remain limited in scope and rely on standard short-read pipelines, resulting in as much as ~20% of common and ~70% of rare HLA alleles being absent from the 1kGP dataset due to limited group sampling, underscoring the incompleteness of current immunogenetic catalogues 17.

text.text: Specialized bioinformatics tools have been developed to infer genotypes at these complex loci from short-read whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23 .

text.text: In parallel, large-scale long-read sequencing efforts by the Human Genome Structural Variation Consortium (HGSVC) and Human Pangenome Reference Consortium (HPRC) have produced sequence-resolved assemblies that improve our understanding of immune receptor variation and provide diverse reference material for benchmarking.
Together, these advances create an opportunity to systematically map immune receptor variation at scale using existing WGS datasets.
Here we present the Global Atlas of Immune Alleles (GAIA), the largest map of immune receptor gene allele frequencies to date.

We analyzed WGS data from over 20,000 individuals across Africa, Asia, the Americas, Oceania, and Europe, with particular emphasis on sub-Saharan Africa (n = 6,163), Island Southeast Asia (n = 2,536), and the Pacific Islands (n = 4,095).

After benchmarking specialized genotyping tools against haplotype-resolved reference assemblies, we calculated allele frequencies stratified by geographic groups and identify alleles whose frequencies diverge substantially from the Allele Frequency Net Database (AFND), or for which we provide the first frequency estimate 1 .

text.text: To quantify how immune diversity is distributed within groups, we introduce majority allelic diversity (MAD-X), defined as the number of alleles selected by a greedy algorithm until at least X% of individuals in a group carry at least one.

Finally, we highlight clinically relevant variation in groups where it has not previously been well-characterized, demonstrating the concrete health consequences of the diversity gaps revealed by GAIA.

To profile immune receptor allele frequency at a global scale, we assembled a diverse cohort of individuals with short-read WGS from multiple publicly available studies and newly generated data from 8,463 individuals (see Methods).
We recognize that human genetic variation is continuous and does not fall neatly into discrete groups.
However, in order to describe the global distribution of allele frequencies for the purposes of this study, we grouped individuals by continental (e.g.
Africa, Oceania, Europe, etc.) and subcontinental (e.g.
Northern, Western, Eastern, etc.) regions and calculated allele frequencies within these groupings (see Supplemental Table S1 for group definitions).

text.text: We compared HLA allele frequencies in GAIA with those reported in the AFND to assess how allele frequencies in historically underrepresented groups differ from those currently catalogued.
For each identified allele, we computed a GAIA-wide frequency, compared it with the corresponding AFND frequency, and identified the most differential alleles.

These results highlight how even modest increases in global representation in allele discovery can uncover substantial novel frequency information.
Although the largest portion of genetic immunology research has centered on HLA, the immune response is dictated by a host of genes and mechanisms.
Genes belonging to the IGHC and FCGR families have been implicated in disease-related outcomes 29, 30, 31, 32 but their diversity is less well documented and cataloged.

text.text: The absence of these efforts can be seen in the benchmarking results where the genotyping accuracy for genes within these families is generally lower than what is observed in the major HLA subcomplexes and in the smaller number of alleles used in our genotyping databases (average 55 per IGHC gene vs 1,180 per HLA gene).
Despite this limitation, we note large differences in the most abundant allele per subcontinental group for the IGHC genes.

text.text: This pattern was not observed across FCGR2 or FCGR3 genes.

Some technical factors could complicate the analysis: FCGR1A and FCGR1B have the lowest benchmarking performance in the FCGR locus, and this allele set is drawn specifically from alleles in the HPRC graph, so the signal could stem from underrepresentation of Pacific Islander individuals in the graph.
The significance of the results for IGHC and FCGR are not yet understood, but we report them to encourage future research.
Understanding global diversity has a direct impact on health initiatives, not least of which is vaccine design.

Achieving broad protective coverage and evaluating safety in epitope-based vaccine design typically requires targeting alleles sufficient to cover at least 90% of individuals in a group 35 , with earlier work establishing 80% coverage from 3-5 molecules per ethnicity but requiring different specificities in each 36 ; population coverage is conventionally computed from HLA genotype frequencies and epitope restriction data 37 .
text.formatted: Achieving broad protective coverage and evaluating safety in epitope-based vaccine design typically requires targeting alleles sufficient to cover at least 90% of individuals in a group <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">35</ref> , with earlier work establishing 80% coverage from 3-5 molecules per ethnicity but requiring different specificities in each <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">36</ref> ; population coverage is conventionally computed from HLA genotype frequencies and epitope restriction data 37 .

text.text: Existing diversity metrics summarize variation at a locus as a single value 38 , but do not directly indicate how many alleles must be included to reach a given level of population coverage.

To make such comparisons tractable, we introduce majority allelic diversity (MAD-X), defined as the number of alleles selected by a greedy algorithm until at least X% of individuals in a group carry at least one.

MAD provides a direct measure of how concentrated or dispersed allelic diversity is: at lower thresholds (MAD-50) it quantifies how few alleles suffice to reach half of a group, and at thresholds relevant to vaccine design (MAD-90) it quantifies the breadth of alleles required to achieve broad group coverage.

To illustrate this point, we focus on the HLA-B locus which shows the highest MAD-50 among the HLA genes with a mean of 4.8 between continental groups (Figure 3A), consistent with prior findings that HLA-B is the most diverse HLA subcomplex and with evidence that HLA-B dominates CD8+ T cell recognition and immune selection where locus-specific contributions have been directly measured 39, 40, 41 .

text.text: While MAD-50 captures where common diversity is concentrated, MAD-90 therefore provides a direct quantification of the allelic breadth required for equitable vaccine design at each locus and in each group.
The HLA-B locus had a mean MAD-90 of 16.2 between continental groups, followed by DRB1, C, and A with mean MAD-90 values of 10.8, 9.2, and 8.4 respectively (Figure 3B).

The ratio of MAD-90 to MAD-50 provides a measure of how heavy the tail of common variation is at each locus.

For HLA-B, across subcontinental groups, this ratio spanned from 5.3 in Island Southeast Asia to 2.7 in Northern Africa, revealing that the alleles required for broad coverage outnumber those that account for the bulk of the group (Figure 3F).

text.text: These findings indicate that the operational cost of designing globally equitable T cell vaccines is concentrated at HLA-B and falls disproportionately on groups whose diversity is least represented in current reference databases.

text.text: Organizing these findings by clinical actionability revealed three categories: (1) confirmatory observations that validate established group-allele patterns at unprecedented resolution, (2) alleles indicating that current pharmacogenomic guidance may be miscalibrated for specific groups, and (3) disease-associated alleles common in groups where they have not previously been well-characterized (Figure 4, Supplemental Table S10).

text.text: Validation of established group-allele patterns.
GAIA recapitulates a number of well-established group-specific allele distributions at a larger scale than originally reported.
The African continental group carries a group of HLA-B alleles known to modulate HIV-1 disease outcomes, particularly for the subtype C virus that predominates in sub-Saharan Africa.

These include B*57:03, the class I allele most strongly associated with suppression of HIV without the use of antiretroviral therapy 42, 43, 44, 45 ; B*81:01 and B*58:01, which mediate protection through Gag-restricted CD8+ T cell responses 46, 47, 48, 49, 50 ; and B*42:01, which is genetically related to B*81:01 but confers more modest protection 51 .

text.text: The protective B*57:02 subtype was observed at greater than 1% frequency in the Eastern African group (1.4% [95% CI: 1.0-1.7%]).

Conversely, B*58:02, which is associated with rapid disease progression due to its failure to mount effective Gag-specific immune pressure 52 , is also common only in the African continental group, illustrating that common alleles in this region include those that are both protective and risk-associated (6.4% [95% CI: 5.9-6.8%]).

text.text: These confirmatory observations validate GAIA's recovery of clinically relevant variation and provide the largest-scale frequency estimates to date for these alleles in the groups where they are of high importance.
Group-specific frequencies refine pharmacogenomic guidance.
Pharmacogenomic screening recommendations often use geography or diaspora-based characterization and may benefit from more comprehensive characterization of allele frequencies in GAIA.
Two examples illustrate how this can both under-and over-estimate the group frequency of clinically-actionable alleles.

The Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium (CPIC) recommends HLA-B*57:01 testing in all abacavir-naive patients 57 , but B*57:01 is not detected in Western and Northern African groups in GAIA, consistent with published evidence that universal screening thresholds may not be warranted in these groups 58 .

The combined picture across these regions demonstrates that B*27 typing alone is insufficient for AS risk stratification in Asia-Pacific groups; subtype resolution is required, and the relevant subtypes differ by group.

text.text: GAIA addresses a critical gap in immunogenomics by providing the most complete survey to date of immune gene loci and allele frequencies across genetically diverse and historically underrepresented subcontinental groups, and introduces majority allelic diversity (MAD) as a framework for quantifying the allelic breadth required for equitable group coverage.

Together, the atlas and the metric reveal that current reference databases underestimate the diversity that vaccine design and pharmacogenomic guidance must accommodate, and that this underestimation disproportionately affects groups already underserved by precision medicine.

Our MAD-90 analysis quantifies this challenge directly: achieving 90% group coverage for vaccine development at HLA-B requires 61 alleles in the GAIA cohort overall, and up to 24 alleles in the South American subcontinental group, substantially more than would be inferred from current reference databases.
Notably, the North and South American groups included many admixed individuals, which may contribute to the high MAD-90 values observed.

Admixture averages allele frequencies across source populations weighted by their relative contributions, shifting alleles toward intermediate frequencies and away from fixation, and thus requiring more alleles to reach a given coverage threshold.

The fact that MAD-90 exceeds MAD-50 at HLA-B by a factor of ~2 globally and up to 5.3 on a group-by-group basis indicates that the alleles required for broad protective coverage extend well beyond those that dominate the group, and that this tail is most pronounced in the groups least represented in existing resources.

HLA variation has been shown to drive measurable differences in vaccine antibody response in African groups 73 , underscoring that reference databases skewed toward well-studied groups risk producing vaccines with uneven global coverage.
text.formatted: HLA variation has been shown to drive measurable differences in vaccine antibody response in African groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">73</ref> , underscoring that reference databases skewed toward well-studied groups risk producing vaccines with uneven global coverage.

text.text: MAD-90 makes that risk quantifiable, and identifies HLA-B as the locus where the operational cost of equitable design is concentrated.
The atlas itself contributes a 38% increase in the number of alleles with frequency information in the AFND, while comprising fewer than 0.5% of the total observations in the database.

This rate of discovery indicates that representation, not sample size alone, is the limiting factor for completing global immunogenetic catalogues, and that even modest expansions of the GAIA dataset are likely to reveal further novel allele frequency information for the remaining 30,651 (80.5%) IPD-IMGT/HLA 74 classified alleles for which no group-level frequency data currently exist.
text.formatted: This rate of discovery indicates that representation, not sample size alone, is the limiting factor for completing global immunogenetic catalogues, and that even modest expansions of the GAIA dataset are likely to reveal further novel allele frequency information for the remaining 30,651 (80.5%) IPD-IMGT/HLA <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">74</ref> classified alleles for which no group-level frequency data currently exist.

text.text: GAIA is a first step toward closing the gap in our understanding of how these alleles shape health outcomes and interact with one another and with environmental factors.
GAIA offers a more equitable approach to allele frequency estimates but remains subject to sampling bias arising from study design (e.g., cohorts recruited under specific clinical conditions).

While our MAD metrics quantify the scope of common immune diversity and reveal distinct patterns across less well-studied subcomplexes, linking specific alleles to functional outcomes in underrepresented groups will require further research that incorporates direct clinical or immunological measurements.

MAD also counts alleles rather than epitopes; because individual peptides frequently bind multiple alleles within an allelic family or supertype, MAD-90 bounds the number of distinct binding specificities a vaccine must accommodate rather than the number of peptides it must contain 75.
text.formatted: MAD also counts alleles rather than epitopes; because individual peptides frequently bind multiple alleles within an allelic family or supertype, MAD-90 bounds the number of distinct binding specificities a vaccine must accommodate rather than the number of peptides it must contain <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">75</ref>.

text.text: The clinical and genetic findings highlighted here focus on HLA alleles in part because the IGHC and FCGR loci lack a centralized resource analogous to AFND and IPD-IMGT/HLA, but also because the health implications of IGHC variation in particular remain less well-characterized than those of HLA despite similar allelic diversity 76 .
text.formatted: The clinical and genetic findings highlighted here focus on HLA alleles in part because the IGHC and FCGR loci lack a centralized resource analogous to AFND and IPD-IMGT/HLA, but also because the health implications of IGHC variation in particular remain less well-characterized than those of HLA despite similar allelic diversity <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">76</ref> .

text.text: Establishing a unified database for IGHC and FCGR would enable systematic comparison of allele frequencies across groups and, alongside continued functional study, provide a foundation for understanding these genes' roles in disease susceptibility and treatment response.

While the derivation of these results from short-read WGS provides advantages over other methods, there is an inherent limitation to this technology specifically in high homology and copy number variable regions.
New technologies and resources will continue to enable a more complete assessment of immune gene diversity.
Long-read sequencing and high-fidelity assembly techniques can resolve complex loci and have revealed many novel alleles and structural haplotypes in IGH, IGK, and IGL loci 77, 78 .
text.formatted: Long-read sequencing and high-fidelity assembly techniques can resolve complex loci and have revealed many novel alleles and structural haplotypes in IGH, IGK, and IGL loci <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">77,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">78</ref> .

text.text: For instance, a study of IGH 77 identified 130 previously undocumented alleles not present in reference databases.

Long-read assemblies from HGSVC have also demonstrated near-perfect HLA-typing while resolving previously incomplete HLA allele annotations and uncovering novel structural variation affecting genes such as HLA-DPA2 78 .
text.formatted: Long-read assemblies from HGSVC have also demonstrated near-perfect HLA-typing while resolving previously incomplete HLA allele annotations and uncovering novel structural variation affecting genes such as HLA-DPA2 <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">78</ref> .

text.text: These approaches will enable more complete characterization of complex genetic variation at these loci, including copy number and structural variation, and, coupled with richer health data, will improve our ability to link immune gene variation to health outcomes.
Understanding the full breadth of human immune diversity is not only an academic exercise in equity but a measurable prerequisite for global precision public health.

MAD-90 provides one way to make that prerequisite concrete: it tells us how many alleles a vaccine, a screening guideline, or an association study must accommodate to serve a given group, and it shows that current reference databases systematically underestimate that number for most of the world.

Closing that gap is a tractable problem, and GAIA demonstrates that even modest investments in representation yield substantial returns. to maximize population coverage in vaccine design with application to SARS-CoV-2.

text.text: Determining the effect of sequencing depth of coverage on number of newly observed alleles: Due to the wide range of sequencing depths of coverage included in the entire cohort, we assessed whether low sequencing coverage generates spurious calls that would incorrectly increase the number of newly observed alleles.

To test this, we downsampled the 2,662 individuals from LASI-DAD (part of the South Asian group) to an average depth of coverage of 5× and incorporated those into the results for the rest of the cohort as if these downsampled results were the original calls for this subset.
We selected LASI-DAD for two reasons.

First, it is closely size-matched to the Eastern African group (n = 2,593), which contributes the largest number of newly observed alleles (402), so the two are directly comparable without normalization; the downsampled depth of 5× is also comparable to the median depth of the Eastern African group (5.6×).

Second, LASI-DAD yields few newly observed alleles at full depth despite its size, so the expected true signal is near zero and alleles appearing only after downsampling can be attributed to depth rather than to genuine group-specific diversity.
This makes the comparison maximally sensitive to depth-driven artifacts.
We note that this low baseline is consistent with India already being well represented in the AFND, though the argument below depends only on the observed baseline, not on its cause.
Originally, we reported 37 alleles which are group-specific to South Asia and for which no frequency information was available in the AFND across HLA-A, -B, -C, and -DRB1.
After downsampling, we report 32 such alleles (Supplemental Figure S2A), of which 22 were shared with the full-depth set.

text.text: Ten newly observed alleles were called only in the downsampled set; these fall within a total of 20 alleles of any kind called only in the downsampled set (Supplemental Figure S2C).

text.text: Taking these 10 as an upper bound on depth-driven artifacts in a cohort of ~2,600 samples, low coverage could account for at most ~2.5% of the 402 newly observed alleles in the size-matched Eastern African group.

For low coverage to generate the Eastern African signal, the rate of depth-driven artifacts would need to be roughly 40-fold higher there than observed here at matched sample size and comparable depth.

We therefore interpret the group differences in newly observed alleles as reflecting representation in the AFND rather than sequencing depth: the AFND contains over 50,000 individuals from India alone, compared with just over 1,000 from the entire continent of Africa.

text.text: Benchmarking whole genome vs whole exome sequencing for all loci: In addition to comparisons against gold standard sets, we compared tools for consistency against orthogonal data types.

We counted true/false positives/negatives similar to the gold standard analysis with the WGS serving as the gold standard against which to compare WES.
For WGS, 32 genomic loci showed F1-scores above 0.75 with 31 coming from the HLA gene family.

Analysis with hap-eval revealed a higher level of concordance across all regions due to small mismatches in sequence affecting precision in hap-eval less dramatically as compared to a direct matching of genotype which would result in a precision score of 0 for a sample.

text.text: We introduce majority allelic diversity (MAD) as a measure of allelic breadth within a group.
MAD-X is the number of alleles required for X% of individuals in a group to carry at least one allele from the set.
Carrier status is taken from observed diplotypes rather than inferred from allele frequencies, so no Hardy-Weinberg assumption is made.
This matters in admixed and structured groups, where genotype frequencies depart from the expectation under allele frequencies alone.
The set is built greedily.
Beginning with all genotyped individuals in the group, we select the allele carried by the largest number of them and remove every individual carrying it from the pool.
Carrier counts are then recalculated among the individuals who remain, and the allele carried by the largest number of those is added next.

Selection therefore depends on the residual pool rather than on frequency in the group as a whole: an allele that is common but largely confined to individuals already covered contributes little and may never be selected.
Alleles are added until the cumulative number of individuals covered, as a fraction of the group's original size, reaches or exceeds X%.
MAD-X is the size of the resulting set.
For example, in a group of 100 individuals, suppose 84 carry allele 001.
MAD-50 = 1, since 001 alone exceeds the 50% threshold.
Removing those 84 leaves 16 individuals; of these, 12 carry 002, bringing cumulative coverage to 96.

To extend this to a global measure, we define global MAD-X as the number of unique alleles in the union of all subcontinental MAD-X sets -that is, the total number of alleles needed to simultaneously reach the threshold in every subcontinental group.

It should be noted that these numbers can be highly skewed by unequal sampling and population sizes; these figures are meant to be starting points for approaching understanding diversity and vaccine development.
In order to directly understand the distribution of HLA alleles in a given population, more direct sampling would be required.
Global MAD-50 values represent the total number of unique alleles across all subcontinental MAD-50 sets in GAIA.
Across the eight classical loci surveyed by the AFND, DPA1 has the lowest global MAD-50 (4 alleles).
Other loci show even lower allelic diversity, with 15 loci showing a global MAD-50 of 1 (Supplemental Table S7).
text.formatted: Other loci show even lower allelic diversity, with 15 loci showing a global MAD-50 of 1 (Supplemental Table <ref type="table">S7</ref>).

text.text: All of these exist outside of the scope of alleles reported to the AFND and this diversity is reported in GAIA for the first time.

All of these regions are contained in the HLA family of genes and there are only 9 loci in HLA which show a MAD-50 above 4: A, B, C, DPB1, DQA1, DQB1, DRB1, MICA, and H. All IGHC and FCGR loci we examined had a global MAD-50 greater than 4, however, MAD-50 should not be confused with fixation of specific alleles.

For example, at IGHG1 all subcontinental groups show a MAD-50 between 1 and 3, but there are still alleles which are more common in specific subcontinental groups over others as highlighted in the main text and with a global MAD-50 of 8 (Supplemental Figure S3).

text.text: Among all loci surveyed, FCGBP has the highest global MAD-50 value of 137 followed by FCGR3A and FCGR2C at 118 and 116 respectively.
HLA-B has the highest mean MAD-50 among the MHC genes with a value of 3.72 between subcontinental groups, followed by DRB1, A, and C with mean MAD-50 values of 2.94, 2.44, and 2.33, respectively.
Across all MHC loci, the Southern African, North American, South American, and Eastern African subcontinental groups show the highest mean MAD-50 of 1.41, 1.41, 1.39 and 1.37 respectively.
Across all IGHC loci, the top-four subcontinental group MAD-50 values are the Central African (2.2), Southern African (2.2), North American (2.2), and Western African (2.0) subcontinental groups.
For FCGR loci, the top-four subcontinental group MAD-50 values are seen in South America (17.7), North America (15.9), South Asia (13.2), and Western Africa (11.7).
Another metric for understanding allelic diversity is to simply count the total number of unique alleles which are observed in each subcontinental group.

Eastern African subcontinental groups have the highest number of total alleles observed across all HLA loci with a mean of 47.4 alleles per locus, which is supported by previous studies 33, 34, 35, 36 .

text.text: This Eastern African allele diversity is highly concentrated to A, B, and C with 304, 261, and 347 total alleles respectively.
Notably, this subcontinental group shows the highest number of alleles at HLA-DPB1 (199), a locus with a median of 34.0 alleles per group.

Estimating the effect of group size on MAD: In order to determine the effect that group size has on MAD, we ran a series of simulations based on the underlying data to see if trends remained after equalizing group sizes.
We sampled with replacement all subcontinental groups down to 30 individuals per group and calculated allele frequency and MAD statistics for each group (Supplemental Figure S7).
text.formatted: We sampled with replacement all subcontinental groups down to 30 individuals per group and calculated allele frequency and MAD statistics for each group (Supplemental Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_16">S7</ref>).

text.text: We repeated this simulation 1,000 times and empirically derived a 95% confidence interval based on the values observed in the simulations.

While the exact numbers derived from the simulated MAD analysis did not match the values observed in the GAIA dataset, the conclusions derived from the simulations were the same: HLA-B was the most variable region based on MAD-50 and MAD-90 as well as AMRS, AMRN, and AFRE being the most variable subcontinental groups based on MAD-50 and MAD-90.
One exception is made for the ratio of MAD-90:MAD-50 which does not show the same sort order as the observed ratio in the main text.
This is likely due to the fact that MAD-90 values in a simulated small group derived from a diverse group are likely to be depressed due to a bottleneck artifact of the simulation.
In a diverse group, much of the total frequency mass is spread across many rare alleles.
Downsampling is more likely to miss rare alleles entirely and the few alleles that do survive the bottleneck are the ones that were already relatively common.
In a less diverse group, most alleles are already at moderate frequency and survive the downsampling more or less intact and the shape of the frequency distribution is better preserved.

To obtain confidence intervals for the allele frequencies we resampled alleles with replacement randomly from the pool of observed alleles within each subcontinental group, drawing alleles equal to the original group size.
For each of 1,000 bootstrap replicates, the pool of alleles was established and then allele frequency was calculated from the simulated pool.
We then derived 95% confidence intervals for both allele frequencies and MAD values using the percentile method, taking the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the resulting bootstrap distributions.
Similarly, for MAD we established a pool of individuals equal to the group size and calculated MAD from that pool over 1,000 bootstrap replicates.

Integration of Novel Allele Calls: T1K claims the ability to produce novel allele calls via single nucleotide variants relative to the alleles in the given database.

The primary callset only integrates these novel calls when they result in an exact match to the coding sequence of any other IMGT allele and an absence of a match to the original predicted allele's coding sequence.

While this analysis allowed for calling of alleles which were added in a newer IMGT release (v3.63 vs v3.59), novel calls were also integrated if they resulted in a match to another allele which was already in the current database.
The validation of this method can be found below in the section "Validation of Novel Allele Calls".

Figure 3.
Majority allelic diversity (MAD) quantifies the allelic breadth required for group coverage.
A-B) Number of alleles to ensure 50% (MAD-50, A) or 90% (MAD-90, B) of individuals in a group carry at least one allele from the set across HLA-A, -B, -C, and -DRB1 for each continental group.

Both HLA*LA and T1K performed well with F1-scores above 0.73 at HLA-A, -B, -C and DRB1.
At 5× coverage, T1K consistently outperformed HLA*LA across HLA-A, B, and C with an F1-score of 0.80 compared to 0.76 for HLA*LA.

text.text: At 30×, T1K of HLA Loci: We genotyped classical HLA class I (A, B, C), class II (DPA1, DPB1, DQA1, DQB1, DRB1, DRB3, DRB4), non-classical HLA class I (E, F, G), and other MHC loci (MICA, MICB, TAP1, TAP2) using two different tools: T1K and HLA*LA.
Additional HLA loci were called with T1K only (DMA, DMB, DOA, DOB, DPA2, DPB2, DQA2, DQB2, DRA, DRB5, H, HFE, J, K, L, N, P, R, S, T, U, V, W, Y).
These tools were run with default parameters.

HLA*LA makes use of a pangenome graph with IMGT nomenclature which can be found here: http://www.well.ox.ac.uk/downloads/PRG_MHC_GRCh38_withIMGT.tar.gz and T1K took as an input IMGT coding sequences for each locus.
Each coding sequence was padded with 200 base pairs of intronic sequence and joined with N's where intronic gaps were not spanned.
T1K
Gamma Receptors:We genotyped genes in the Fc Gamma Receptor gene family using Locityper and a pre-release version of the HPRC v2.0 graph.

FCGR1A, FCGR1BP, FCGR2A, FCGR2B, FCGR2C, FCGR3A, FCGR3B, and FCGBP were genotyped in GRCh38 coordinates using the following graph: https://s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/human-pangenomics/pangenomes/scratch/2025_02_28_ minigraph_cactus/hprc-v2.0-mc-grch38/hprc-v2.0-mc-grch38.raw.vcf.gz.

Due to an exceedingly large variant spanning the FCGRT locus in the GRCh38-based graph, this gene was genotyped in the hs1-based graph using the following resource: s3://human-pangenomics/pangenomes/scratch/2025_02_28_minigraph_cactus/hprc-v2.0-mc-ch m13/hprc-v2.0-mc-chm13.raw.vcf.gz.
Both graphs were then processed according to the best practices explained in: https://locityper.vercel.app/input_output.
After graph processing, reference k-mer counting, and locus addition, raw reads were then pre-processed and genotyped with default parameters.
